extract:
Curtis James Jackson III, known professionally as 50 Cent, was born in 1975 in the South Jamaica neighborhood of Queens, New York. Raised largely by his grandparents after his mother's death when he was a child, he grew up immersed in the same Queens hip-hop ecosystem that produced Run-DMC, LL Cool J, and Nas. He began rapping in the late 1990s under the mentorship of Jam Master Jay of Run-DMC, who reportedly taught him song structure and helped him land his first deal. His active recording career stretches from the late 1990s to the present, though his commercial peak was concentrated in the first decade of the 2000s.

His earliest major-label work came through Columbia in 1999, where he recorded the unreleased album Power of the Dollar; the controversial single How to Rob, in which he joked about mugging various famous rappers, made him notorious almost overnight. After being shot nine times outside his grandmother's home in 2000, he was dropped by Columbia and spent the next two years building a fearsome reputation through a flood of mixtapes, including Guess Who's Back? and 50 Cent Is the Future, recorded with his crew G-Unit (Lloyd Banks, Tony Yayo, and later Young Buck). These tapes caught the attention of Eminem, who signed him in a joint deal with Shady Records, Aftermath, and Interscope.

His 2003 debut Get Rich or Die Tryin', executive produced by Eminem and Dr. Dre, was a cultural phenomenon, selling over 800,000 copies in its first week and producing the singles In da Club, 21 Questions with Nate Dogg, P.I.M.P., and Many Men (Wish Death). The album's blend of Dre's polished West Coast production with 50's menacing, melodic Queens delivery essentially defined mainstream rap for a moment. Beg for Mercy, the G-Unit group album, followed later that year. His 2005 follow-up The Massacre was nearly as successful, anchored by Candy Shop, Disco Inferno, and Just a Lil Bit, and his very public feud with Ja Rule and Murder Inc. helped cement his dominance over the New York rap scene of the era.

Subsequent albums Curtis (2007) and Before I Self Destruct (2009) sold well but received cooler reviews, and his famous first-week sales battle with Kanye West's Graduation in September 2007 is often cited as a symbolic turning point in hip-hop, with Kanye's win signaling a shift away from the gangsta-rap aesthetic 50 had popularized. He had already diversified by then, taking an equity stake in Vitamin Water before Coca-Cola's 2007 acquisition of Glacéau, a deal that reportedly netted him a fortune and rewrote the playbook for rapper endorsements. His G-Unit Records label released projects by Banks, Yayo, Buck, Mobb Deep, and others.

In recent years 50 Cent has focused more on television and film production through his G-Unit Film & Television company, most notably the Power franchise on Starz, which he executive produces and occasionally appears in, along with its spinoffs Power Book II: Ghost, Raising Kanan, and Force, and the BMF series. He still tours and releases occasional singles, but his legacy rests on a roughly five-year run that produced one of the best-selling rap debuts ever and reshaped the commercial template of the genre.
title: 50 Cent
